1:
Bildad had twice opened his assaults with a weary How long — once at ch. 8:2 and again at ch. 18:2 — and the witnesses notice that Job, having heard him out in silence, now takes up that very weapon and turns it back. The reformed John Gill marks the plain fact of the verse: Job let Bildad finish his oration without interruption, and then rose in his own defence and put in his answer as follows. It is the posture of a man who will not be shouted down but will have his say in order.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the coming reply a wounded man telling his friends how ill he took their severe censure, that because he was so grievously afflicted he must be wicked. What is not liked, Henry observes, is commonly thought long; and Job had more reason to think them long who assaulted him than they had to think him long who only vindicated himself, for better cause may be shown for defending ourselves, if we have right on our side, than for offending our brethren, though we have right on our side. Bildad had begun both his speeches with a How long, and now Job, being to answer him particularly, begins with a How long too, matching the very taunt back upon its author. Yet Henry lets the caution hang over the whole speech: those who enter into disputation enter into temptation to magnify themselves and vilify their brethren more than is fit, and ought to watch and pray against the workings of pride.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sketches the ground the chapter will cover, and it is a wide one: Job complains of the cruelty of his friends, pathetically laments his sufferings, mourns that he is forsaken by servants, kinsfolk, intimates, and even his wife, calls upon his friends to pity him, longs that his words might be recorded, and rises at last to the great confession of hope. The reply thus moves from bitter complaint to the highest reach of faith in the whole book, and this opening verse is only the man clearing his throat to begin. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job answers not as a culprit caught out but as a defendant wronged, and that the How long he is about to utter is the just protest of a sufferer who has borne, on top of God's hand, the added blows of his comforters.
2:
Job's first stroke is the complaint that his friends have wounded not merely his body but his very self: how long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? The reformed John Gill weighs which vexation is the worst. Many things vex good men — pains of body, loss of substance, the emptiness of all earthly enjoyments, the corruptions of their own hearts, the temptations of Satan, the conversation of the wicked; but here the sting is that Job is vexed by his own friends, who of all men should have eased him, and vexed to his very heart. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, had put it that the vexation of the soul is more grievous than the vexation of the bones (Ps. 6:2): they came pretending to comfort and counsel him, yet set themselves to rob him of the only comfort left him in a good God, a good conscience, and a good name, and broke him in pieces with words that were hard and cruel.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch justify the outburst by its very form, calling it a well-earned quousque tandem. Job, enduring unutterable agony both of body and of spirit, and stretched on the rack besides by the united strength of the three, may fairly begin his answer with a how long; the controversy itself is torture to his spirit, and the words he chooses carry the weight of a man crushed and pounded by speech.

The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, notes that Job here begins exactly as Bildad himself had begun, and for good reason: Bildad's last speech had been so offensive and unfeeling, and had infused so much personal malice into its charges, that Job may well ask how long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the indictment of the friends to a point: everything irritating, vexatious, and opprobrious they had recourse to, in order to prop up their own system and overwhelm him; not one of them seems ever to have been touched with a feeling of tenderness, nor does a kind expression drop at any time from their lips. They are called friends, Clarke says, but the word here can only mean cold-blooded acquaintances. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the deepest cruelty in the debate has been the friends' words, and that a soul so vexed has earned the right to protest.
3:
The reproach has not been a single lapse but a settled habit, and Job counts it: these ten times have ye reproached me. The reformed John Gill is careful that the number is not an exact tally but a round figure for many times, in the manner of Scripture elsewhere; it is the lot of good men in every age to be reproached for righteousness' sake, but to be reproached by friends, and reproached as a hypocrite and a wicked man, is the cutting thing, and its frequent repetition aggravates both the friends' sin and Job's affliction and patience together.

The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh the last clause, that his friends make themselves strange to him. Adam Clarke reads it against the backdrop of Job's former prosperity: when he was in affluence they were his intimates and seemed to rejoice in his happiness, but now they scarcely know him, or profess to reckon him wicked because he is in adversity — a suspicion they had never entertained while he flourished; circumstances, Clarke observes drily, change men's minds. He too fixes the ten times as many times rather than an arithmetical count, referring the reader to the same idiom at Gen. 31:7. John Wesley agrees on both points — ten is a certain number put for an uncertain, and to make themselves strange is to carry themselves like strangers to him and condemn him as if they had never known his integrity.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the aggravations Job lays up: they had reproached him often, giving him a bad character and laying to his charge things he knew not, which to an ingenuous mind is a cutting thing; and they were not ashamed of it. They had reason, Henry says, to blush for their hard-heartedness, so ill becoming men, their uncharitableness, so ill becoming good men, and their deceitfulness, so ill becoming friends; yet though told of it again and again, they could not blush. He owns too a fault on Job's side that honesty must name: to keep so exact a reckoning of injuries — these ten times — is peevish and unfriendly, and looks like a design of retaliation, whereas we better befriend our own peace by forgetting unkindnesses than by scoring them up. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the just grief of a man reproached past bearing, even while Henry gently marks the peevishness that a scrupulous count of wrongs betrays.
4:
Job now grants, for argument's sake, the very thing his friends charge, and shows how little it would prove: be it indeed that I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself. The reformed John Gill is careful that this is a concession and not a confession; Job does not own the guilt they allege, though he freely allows that good men may err — in judgment, in practice, in word — for it is human to err, and no man is so perfect as never to mistake in speech. Supposing then that he had erred, Job's point is that the error stays with him: it is his own, not imposed on others as his friends impose theirs, and it is he, not they, who must smart for it.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press that lonely bearing of the fault. Adam Clarke has Job say, suppose indeed I have in the simplicity of my heart gone astray, this error — whatever it is, for there is no public stain on my life — has hurt no person except myself; why then treat me as one whose whole life has been a blot and whose example is a public curse? John Wesley puts it more tenderly still: if I have sinned, I myself suffer for my sins, and therefore deserve your pity rather than your reproaches.

That note of self-suffering carries the puritan reading as well, for Matthew Henry had ranked the errors of Job's judgment among the things capable of excuse which the friends ought to have considered. It is folly, Henry says, to think ourselves infallible; humanity and error cleave together, and we must be willing to suppose the possibility concerning ourselves. Men's mistakes are the more excusable if they keep them to themselves and do not disturb others with them — hast thou faith? have it to thyself. Job, on this reading, imposes his opinion on no one, but only proves his own work by it, meddling with no man either to teach him or to judge him; and if he be in an error, the affliction that error has drawn down is punishment enough, so that his friends need not add the misery of their reproaches to the smart he already feels. It is he, and not they, that must smart for it, and he does smart, and smart severely. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that even granting Job wrong, his supposed error is private, self-punishing, and no warrant for the friends to turn his affliction into an accusation. The concession is a shield, not a surrender.
5:
Job foresees that his friends will not be content to answer him but must tower over him, and he names the temper: if indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead against me my reproach. The reformed John Gill catches the swagger in the words — the friends look and talk big, set themselves up as great folk, resolve to run him down, open their mouths wide in a blustering manner, and magnify what they are pleased to call his error, setting it out in the worst light they can. It is the posture of men determined to win the argument by loudness where they cannot win it by justice.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had already fastened on this magnifying as one of the unkindnesses Job most keenly felt. His friends not only estranged themselves from him but magnified themselves against him; they not only looked shy of him but looked big upon him, and insulted over him, magnifying themselves on purpose to depress him. It is a mean thing, Henry says, it is a base thing, thus to trample upon those that are down — and baser still to do it under the colour of piety, as if pride against a broken man were zeal for God. He hears in Job's how long the complaint of a sufferer resolved that his comforters seemed resolved to persist: those that speak too much seldom think they have said enough, and when the mouth is opened in passion the ear is shut to reason.

The deeper charge lies in the second clause, that they plead against him his reproach — that is, they make his very affliction the argument that he is wicked. Henry weighs this as the height of their injustice: they should have pleaded his integrity for him, and helped him take the comfort of it under his trouble, as Paul pleaded the testimony of a good conscience in 2 Cor. 1:12; instead they plead his reproach against his integrity, which is not only unkind but unjust, for where shall we find an honest man if his reproach may be admitted as a plea against him? The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job bracing himself against friends who will make his misery their evidence, and who mistake the swelling of their own words for the vindication of God. Against that hard temper Job sets, in the next breath, the true author of his trouble.
6:
Before his friends draw another conclusion from his ruin, Job would have them fix the author of it: know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net. The reformed John Gill reads the demand as a caution: let them take notice that all his afflictions are from the hand of God, whose ways are unsearchable, and take care to what they impute the acts of one whom God has cast down from a high estate to a very low one. The word, Gill allows, may also be rendered hath perverted me, yet not as though God had made Job perverse or perverted his cause; Job could answer Bildad's own question — doth God pervert judgment? — with a firm no, while still owning that it was God's hand, and no accident, that overthrew him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the net and unfolds it with his usual antiquarian relish. The matter, he says, lies between God and Job, and God has not commissioned the friends to add their reproaches to his chastisements; and the image of being encompassed with a net recalls an ancient mode of combat, the Roman retiarius who cast his net over his adversary's head and dragged him down with a noose, while the secutor pursued with sword and shield; the Persians used a running loop, the kumund, and the Goths a hoop-net flung over horse or man to haul them in. To such a device Job likens the encircling providence that has caught and pulled him down.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears Job answering Bildad's substance without quoting his words, for Bildad had said much of the wicked being snared by his own sin; Job replies that it is God who has taken him in his net and compassed him about, an assertion he has made before at ch. 16:7 and ch. 13:27. Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, draws the pastoral point Job is pressing: his trouble was very great, he was overthrown and could not help himself, enclosed as in a net and unable to get out; and God was the author of it. Let God's controversy with me be ended, Henry has him say, before you begin yours; it is barbarous to persecute him whom God has smitten, and to talk to the grief of one whom he has wounded (Ps. 69:26). The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job traces every stroke to God's hand, and asks his friends, before they judge, to reckon with whose net it is that holds him.
7:
Caught in that net, Job cries and finds no answer: behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard. The reformed John Gill takes the wrong as violence or injury — the plundering of his substance by Sabean and Chaldean, the assault on his health by Satan — which he complains of as in open court, as a violation of justice, and cries out against in prayer to God, yet without redress. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes the two ends of the cry: it is uttered unto God, and the wrong is chiefly this, that he is oppressed by his own friends; so that the verse gathers both the divine silence and the human unkindness into one lament.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the complaint in its larger design, for the description Job now gives of himself as persecuted and forsaken by God is needed to enhance the value of the confession he is about to make. Severely has God dealt with him, yet that very severity has only drawn him nearer and made him trust the more. Here Ellicott sees Job group a rich variety of figures for his desolation: he is suffering assault and can get no protection or redress; he is imprisoned on every side; his hope is torn up like the tree of which he had spoken at ch. 14:7. Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps it short and sharp: I complain of violence and of injustice, but no one comes to my help.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the pathos of the unanswered cry into a word of comfort for the like-afflicted. Job complained of his pain but got no ease; he begged to know the cause of his affliction but could not discover it; he appealed to God's tribunal for the clearing of his innocency but could not obtain a hearing, much less a judgment upon his appeal. God, Henry says, may for a time seem to turn away his ear from his people, to be angry at their prayers and overlook their appeals; and they must be excused if in that case they complain bitterly, for woe unto us if God be against us. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the groan of a man doubly forsaken, unheard by the God he cries to and unhelped by the friends who should plead for him — and they agree that this depth is drawn on purpose, that the height of his coming confession may shine the brighter against it.
8:
He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths — and the witnesses read the double image as the shutting-up of a traveller with no road left, forward or back. The reformed John Gill draws the figure out at length: the people of God are pilgrims and travellers through this world, and though their way is for the most part passable, sometimes God builds a very wall against them, encloses them with hewn stones, and so fences up the road that they cannot get through; difficulties present themselves that seem insurmountable, and they stand still, not knowing what course to steer. Job feels himself so walled in that he can neither extricate himself from his troubles nor so much as see a way through them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of the strophe in which Job traces stroke after stroke to God — the fenced way, the darkened paths, the stripped glory, the uprooted hope, the kindled wrath, the encamping troops — reading it as the opening note of a sustained lament that God himself has hedged and besieged him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, keeping to his military and hunting frame, hears in the fencing-up of the way the language either of the great beast driven and hemmed in the chase, or of an invading army that has seized all the passes so that the enemy is cut off and cannot move.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as Job looking forward for deliverance and seeing that hope too cut off. He hath fenced up my way, that I cannot pass; I have now no way left to help myself, either to get out of my troubles or to ease myself under them; and if I would please myself with the prospect of a deliverance hereafter, I cannot, for it is not only out of my reach but out of my sight — God hath set darkness in my paths, and there is none to tell me how long, as the psalmist mourned in Ps. 74:9. Henry hears in it a man who complains not that the road is hard but that it is closed, and closed by the very hand he had trusted to open it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job feels himself God's prisoner, walled in and benighted, unable to advance to relief or retreat to his former peace — and that the darkness he laments is the more grievous because it falls across the path of one who once walked in the light of God's countenance.
9:
The stripping of a plundered traveller supplies the next figure: he hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head. The reformed John Gill keeps the metaphor of the man fallen among thieves and stripped of his clothes, but is careful to say what glory Job means. Not his spiritual glory — not the robe of righteousness nor the graces that make the saints all glorious within, for of these he was not stripped — but his glory in a civil sense: his wealth and substance, his numerous family, his rich apparel and stately house, everything that made him magnificent among men. Whoever were the instruments, Gill says, Job ascribes the loss wholly to God's sovereign hand.

The wesleyan-arminian voices fill out the inventory. John Wesley reads the glory as Job's estate, children, authority, and all his comforts, and the crown as all his power, now that God has laid his honour in the dust. Adam Clarke states it barely and feelingly: I am reduced to such circumstances that I have lost all my honour and respect. The crown, in Job's mouth, is no royal diadem but the dignity and esteem a great man wore among his people, plucked now from his head as a conqueror plucks the crown from a captive king; Gill too keeps the figure of the plundered traveller, adding that whatever made Job magnificent among men — abundance of goods, a numerous family, fine apparel, a stately house — was now stripped from him by one means or another, and all of it ascribed to God's sovereign hand.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the losses into a meditation on the vanity of worldly glory. Did Job look back upon his former prosperity? He saw God's hand putting an end to it: he has stripped me of my glory, my wealth, honour, power, and all the opportunity I had of doing good. My children were my glory, but I have lost them; and whatever was a crown to my head he has taken it from me, and laid all my honour in the dust. See, Henry says, the vanity of worldly glory: it is what we may be soon stripped of, and whatever strips us, we must see and own God's hand in it and comply with his design. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the glory Job mourns is the outward and losable kind, and that the very naming of it as God's doing keeps the complaint from despair — for the God who took the crown is the God Job will presently confess as his living Redeemer, in whom a better and unfading glory is laid up.
10:
He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree — and the witnesses hear in the words the total ruin of a man attacked from every quarter at once. The reformed John Gill reads the destruction on every side of Job's whole estate and person: his oxen and asses on one hand, his camels on another, his sheep and his children each in their turn, all demolished in a single day; and his own body too, smitten with ulcers from crown to sole, this earthly tabernacle falling down on every side. The figure of the removed hope he takes from a tree dug about on all sides, its roots laid bare and its fibres cut, so that it is utterly destroyed from growing.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the finality of that uprooting. Adam Clarke: there is no more hope of restoration to affluence, authority, and respect than there is that a tree should grow again whose roots are torn out of the earth — I am pulled up by the roots, withered, and gone. John Wesley reads every side as Job's person, family, and estate together, and I am gone as the cry of a lost and dead man; his hope of all present things is gone, yet not, Wesley adds, his hope of the life to come. For a tree once plucked up by the roots never grows again, and hope in this life is a perishing thing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry meets Wesley on that hopeful qualification and turns it into comfort. Job saw God's troops destroying him on every side; time was when God's hosts encamped round about him for safety — hast thou not made a hedge about him? — and now they surrounded him to his terror. He concludes himself quite lost and undone for this world, his hope removed like a tree cut down or plucked up by the roots. But hope in this life, Henry says, though a perishing thing, is with good men only removed like a tree, transplanted from this nursery to the garden of the Lord; we have no reason to complain if God thus remove our hopes from the sand to the rock, from things temporal to things eternal. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job here reckons himself finished as to this world, and that the very completeness of the ruin sets off the wonder of the hope he will confess — a hope that even an uprooted tree cannot lose when its root is in God.
11:
From the ruin of his estate Job turns to the temper he thinks he reads behind it: he hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies. The reformed John Gill notes that the metaphor now shifts to a state of open warfare, in which enemies are engaged in hostile array; Job imagined that the wrath of God, comparable to fire for its force and fury, was kindled against him and bursting into flame, and that the terrors of it were set in battle-array around him — the mistaken apprehension, Gill adds, of many a good man in the dark, who takes his afflictions for tokens of wrath.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the whole passage from v.7 onward as one sustained figure of a hostile invasion, and here fits this verse into its place: a neighbouring chief has fallen without provocation upon Job's territory, seized the passes, carried the regal city by assault, stripped the treasures and the crown, routed the armies in the field, and now, at the height of outrage, wastes everything with fire and sword — he hath kindled his wrath against me, and treateth me like one of his adversaries. The verse marks the point in the campaign where the invader spares nothing. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply anchors the language to Job's earlier cries of being torn and hunted as an enemy at ch. 16:9.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry corrects the very apprehension Job voices, even while feeling its weight. What is the fire of hell, he asks, but the wrath of God? Seared consciences will feel it hereafter but do not fear it now; enlightened consciences fear it now but shall not feel it hereafter. Job's present apprehension was that God counted him as one of his enemies — and yet at that same moment God loved him and gloried in him as his faithful friend. It is a gross but very common mistake, Henry says, to think that whom God afflicts he treats as enemies; whereas, on the contrary, as many as he loves he rebukes and chastens, for it is the discipline of his sons. The witnesses do not divide over the fact of Job's dread; they only, with Henry, gently overrule his reading of it, agreeing that the kindled wrath he feels is real to his conscience but false to his case, and that the God who seemed his besieger was all the while his Father.
12:
The war-figure holds as the besieging host comes up: his troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle. The reformed John Gill reads the troops as Job's afflictions, which are many and follow so fast one upon another that there is scarce an interval between them; they are God's hosts, his soldiers, at his command, so that he says to one Go and it goes, and to another Come and it comes. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in brief: the troops are Job's afflictions, God's soldiers marching under his conduct, and to raise up their way is to cast up a trench or siege-mound round about him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the siege its full and moving shape. Did Job look down upon his present troubles? He saw God giving them their commission and their orders to attack him: they are his troops, that act by his direction, which encamp against him. It did not so much trouble Job that his miseries came in troops as that they were God's troops, in whom it seemed as if God fought against him and intended his destruction. They encamped round about his tabernacle as soldiers lay siege to a strong city, cutting off all provision from being brought in and battering it continually. And Henry draws the sharp reversal that gives the verse its ache: time was when God's hosts encamped round Job for safety — hast thou not made a hedge about him?, the boast of ch. 1:10 — but now, on the contrary, they surrounded him to his terror and destroyed him on every side. Adam Clarke, tracing the same invasion, sets this verse where the beaten prince is cooped up with the wrecks of his army and closely besieged, forts raised against him on every hand.

The witnesses do not divide, and the pathos they share is not in the number of Job's afflictions but in their generalship. An enemy's siege a man might bear; but Job feels the works thrown up against him to be God's own, the hedge that once fenced him turned into a trench that pens him. It is the same hand, he perceives, that raised the wall of protection and now raises the mound of assault; and the whole terror of the verse lies in that identity. The soldiers battering his tabernacle are not strangers but the hosts of the God he served — and yet, as Henry has insisted, the appearance deceives, for the besieging Lord is not in truth his enemy but his afflicting friend.
13:
He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me — and the witnesses hear the war-figure pass into something lonelier, the cutting-off of a man from all human succour. The reformed John Gill keeps the martial image a moment longer: as it is part of the business of war to cut off an enemy from his confederates and allies, so God is here represented as keeping far from Job all from whom he might have looked for comfort — his very brethren, who had natural claims of blood, standing now aloof and showing him no regard; and because this estrangement was itself an effect of the afflicting hand of God, Job ascribes it, like all the rest, to him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks how deep this new wound goes. The sense of human desertion, he says, is hardly less terrible than that of being forsaken by God, and this has now been added to Job. The Psalmist seems to have copied the very line at Ps. 88:8, thou hast put away mine acquaintance far from me; and Ellicott cannot read these sad complaints without seeing how fitly they apply to the sorrows of the Man of Sorrows, so completely did Christ enter into the very heart of human suffering that the deepest expressions of it — whether in Job, in the Psalms of David, or in the Lamentations of Jeremiah — inevitably remind us of him. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, group this verse with those that follow, reading a widening circle of desertion — brethren removed, acquaintance estranged, kinsfolk failing, familiar friends forgetting.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the lesson that reconciles the two hands at work. As we must eye the hand of God in all the injuries we receive from our enemies, so likewise in all the slights and unkindnesses we receive from our friends; and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds the same double truth without excusing the friends. God has put Job's brethren far from him, Henry allows — that is, has laid upon him the afflictions that frighten them away and make them stand aloof from his sores; as it was their sin, God was not the author of it, for it is Satan that alienates men's minds from their brethren in affliction; but as it was Job's trouble, God ordered it for the completing of his trial. Every creature, Henry says, is that to us, kind or unkind, which God makes it to be; yet this does not excuse the horrid ingratitude of those who make themselves strange to a friend in trouble, for a friend loves at all times, and adversity is the proof of friendship. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job feels, beneath the desertion of men, the ordering hand of God, and that to trace the wound thus to its highest cause is what makes it bearable.
14:
The circle of loss draws tighter: my kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. The reformed John Gill weighs the word failed, which can mean to cease or to be no more, and so sometimes signifies death; but here he takes it not of their dying but of their ceasing to be near — those who were near Job in blood and had often been near him in place, in his own house and company, are near him now no longer in affection, having ceased to visit, converse, or sympathize with one whose trouble they will not share. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it more bluntly still: my kinsfolk have departed; they have all left his house, now there is no more hope of gain from him. The kinship that clustered about his prosperity melts away with it.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the failure of the kinsfolk within his long account of Job's forsaking, and feels the particular sting of it. His kinsfolk, who claimed relation to him when he was in prosperity, now failed him; they came short both of their former professions of friendship and of his present just expectation of kindness. Even his familiar friends, whom he had been mindful of, had now forgotten him — forgotten both his former friendliness to them and his present misery; they had heard of his troubles and perhaps designed him a visit, but truly they forgot it, so little affected were they with his case. So uncertain, Henry says, is the friendship of men; but if God be our friend, he will not fail us in a time of need.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of the verse is itself part of its weight. Job does not argue or accuse; he simply records, name by name, the emptying of his world — kinsfolk gone, intimates forgetting — as a man counting the empty chairs at his own table. It is the common experience of the fallen great, that the crowd which gathered round their fortune scatters at their misfortune, and Henry will not let the reader think it strange or new. Let none, he warns, that pretend either to humanity or to religion ever use their friends as Job's friends used him; for adversity is the proof of friendship, and by that proof these had already failed. Yet beneath the lament the witnesses hear the same steadying confession as before: that the God who let the kinsfolk fail is himself the friend who does not, and toward whom Job's hope is even now silently turning.
15:
Job's own household turns on him next: they that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger; I am an alien in their sight. The reformed John Gill takes those that dwell in the house to be neither neighbours nor tenants nor lodgers — unthinkable for the greatest man of the east — but the strangers and proselytes Job had received under his roof in hospitality, giving them lodging, food, and raiment as the law required; and even these, whom his own kindness had sheltered, now reckon their benefactor a foreigner. Gill passes on a tradition preserved by Jerome, that Job's house stood at Carnea, a large village in a corner of Batanea beyond the floods of Jordan; whatever its site, it was full of dependents who now looked through him as through an alien.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the verse as a study in the world's usage of the fallen. Adam Clarke draws out how sharply Job describes the contempt commonly shown to men who have dropped from affluence and authority into poverty: formerly reverenced by all, now esteemed by none; for the rich have many friends, and men worship the rising sun who think little of that which is gone down. He tells the tale of a bishop driven from his see in a persecuting reign, who, greeted mockingly one morning as Bishop quondam — bishop that was — answered smartly, Adieu, knave semper — knave that ever shall be; a fallen man may keep his wit though he lose his place. John Wesley adds only a tender note on the maids, who by reason of their sex commonly have more compassionate hearts than men, so that their coldness cut the deeper.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the whole scene under the master's just expectation of his own household. Ordinarily the head of a family looks to be attended and cared for by those of his house, even when weakness of body or mind has made him despicable to others; but poor Job was misused by his own family, and some of his worst foes were those of his own house. His servants slighted him, his maids did not attend him in his illness but counted him a stranger and an alien. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the estrangement has now crossed Job's own threshold, and that a man abandoned even by the dependents his charity had fed is stripped of the last outward comfort — left, as the chapter is driving him, with no refuge but the God whose hand had touched him.
16:
The neglect grows plainer and more galling: I called my servant, and he gave me no answer; I intreated him with my mouth. The reformed John Gill dwells on all that the words imply. This was a trusty and favoured manservant, one Job had shown much kindness to in his prosperity, and who owed his master ready and cheerful obedience in all things, the more so now that Job lay so grievously afflicted and stood in double need of service. Instead, the servant will not so much as come at his call. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the reversal: the servant who once saw every command in his master's eye and was attentive to his least wink now not only fails to come at his call but returns him no answer at all — the home-born slave, who of all men owed him fidelity, has grown deaf.

The bitterest touch, all the witnesses feel, is in the last clause — that Job must intreat him with his mouth. Keil and Delitzsch render it that Job is obliged to entreat him, a master reduced to begging his own servant. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the pathos of that descent. Job had been a good master, who did not despise the cause of his manservant or maidservant when they pleaded with him, as he would afterward protest at ch. 31:13; and yet now they were rude to him and despised his cause when he pleaded with them. Though sick, he was not cross and imperious with them, as is too common, but entreated his servants with his mouth when he had the authority to command — and still they would not be civil to him, neither kind nor just.

Henry draws from it a rule for the wounded heart. We must not think it strange, he says, if we receive evil at the hand of those from whom we have deserved well; and those that are sick and in sorrow are apt to take things ill, to be jealous of a slight, and to lay to heart the least unkindness. When Job was in affliction, even his servant's neglect of him troubled him. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse measures Job's abasement by the strange spectacle of a great and generous master turned suppliant in his own house, entreating where he might command, and answered only by silence. Every prop of earthly dignity has now been knocked away, and the man who once ruled a household must beg its meanest member for a word.
17:
My breath is strange to my wife, Job says, and the witnesses divide over just what the estrangement is. The reformed John Gill offers three senses and weighs them. It may be his natural breath, grown foul and unsavoury through some inward disorder, so that his wife could not bear to come near him — though Gill doubts this, since if his breath were so offensive his friends could hardly have sat conversing with him so long; or it may be the words of his mouth, his speech, grown disagreeable to her ever since he checked her counsel to curse God and die and taught her to expect evil as well as good at God's hand; or, taking the word as spirit, it may be his very life, wearisome and loathsome to a wife tired out with his groans and wishing him gone.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read on into the harder clause, that Job intreated for the children's sake of his own body, and take it of the confidential circle now turned from him: those to whom he had confided his most secret plans, the men of his counsel, now abhor him, and those whom he had loved and drawn close have turned against him — an allusion, they note, that reaches even to the three friends. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers over the children, and finds in the plea a possible ray: Job may be adjuring his wife by the tenderest ties, by the offspring who had been the seals of their mutual affection; and the mention of children may hint that some yet remained — young ones, perhaps, too little to have been at the fatal feast where the elder perished. Charles Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, would rather render the clause of Job's own affection, so is my kindness to the children of my mother's womb, that is, to his brethren, though he allows the reading that makes Job offensive to them.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the domestic desolation to its lowest point. One would think, he says, that when all forsook him the wife of his bosom should have been tender of him; but because he would not curse God and die, as she had urged, his breath was strange to her too — she did not care to come near him, nor took notice of what he said, though he spoke to her not with the authority but with the tenderness of a husband, entreating her by that conjugal love their children had pledged. It now appeared, Henry adds soberly, that the devil had spared her to Job not only to be his tempter but to be his tormentor. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether the strangeness lie in his breath, his speech, or his very life, all agree that the last and nearest earthly comfort has failed, and that the man is left utterly alone with God.
18:
The contempt spreads even to the streets and the smallest of the town: yea, young children despised me; I arose, and they spake against me. The reformed John Gill turns from Job's own doors to what befell him without. Having told of the coldness of household, maids, servants, and wife, Job now records how young children — little ones who had learned it of their parents, having watched their elders treat him with scorn — mocked and jeered at him, pointing perhaps and saying there sits old Job with his boils and ulcers, or some such contemptuous word. He was jeered by profane persons who would tease him with his religion, ask where his God was now, and bid him observe what all his piety and strict living had come to. The very word for these mockers, Gill notes, is rendered by some fools — not idiots, but fools in the moral sense, who make a mock at sin and a jest of religion, and so think nothing of despising a good man.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fastens on the touching detail of the second clause: I arose — Job rose from his seat to show respect to these children, though they were his inferiors, and for that very courtesy they spoke against him. The old man's civility was answered with insolence; his rising to honour them drew only their railing.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the scene in the same key, reading it of the little children born in Job's house, the children of his own servants, who were his servants by birth and yet despised him and spoke against him; though he arose in civility to speak friendly to them, or with authority to check them, they let him know that they neither feared nor loved him. It is the completing insult of his abasement, Henry implies, that the very youngest and least should feel free to trample on a man so plainly forsaken; when God has withdrawn a man's honour, even children read the withdrawal and presume upon it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, who had been the greatest and most reverenced man of the east, at whose approach the aged rose and princes held their peace, is now openly flouted by babes — the whole ladder of respect inverted, so that the highest is become the scorn of the lowest. And still, under the heaping indignity, the reader feels the pressure that will force from him, a few verses on, the one hope no child's mockery can touch.
19:
The desertion reaches its innermost ring: all my inward friends abhorred me, and they whom I loved are turned against me. The reformed John Gill unfolds the phrase the men of my secret — those so familiar with Job that he imparted to them the secrets of his heart and the most private affairs of his life, treating them as bosom friends; for such confidence is always reckoned a great instance of friendship. And now the minds of these very men are set against him: they abhor the sight of him and decline all conversation with him, and not one of them, Gill stresses, shows him any respect. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in a phrase — his inward friends are his intimates and confidants, to whom he had imparted all his thoughts and counsels — and Adam Clarke, briefly, that they were those who had been his greatest intimates. Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, glosses them precisely as the men of his counsel, familiar with his secret affairs.

The witnesses agree that this is the sharpest turn of all, for it is one thing to be forgotten by kinsfolk and slighted by servants, and another to be abhorred by the men one has loved and trusted with one's heart. Keil and Delitzsch, expounding the same strophe, feel the deliberate ordering of it: Job has moved from the outer circle inward — brethren, acquaintance, kinsfolk, household, wife, children, and now the confidential few — so that the lament closes on the betrayal that lies nearest the bone. Those to whom he had opened his most secret plans now shrink from him, and those whom he had drawn to his side have turned to the other.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds it up as the very measure of unnatural unkindness. His inward friends, the men of his secret whom he was most intimate with and laid in his bosom, not only forgot him but abhorred him, keeping as far off as they could because he was poor and could no longer entertain them, and because he was a loathsome spectacle. Those whom he loved, and who were therefore worse than publicans if they did not love him in his distress, not only turned from him but were turned against him, doing all they could to make him odious, so to justify their own strangeness to him. So uncertain is the friendship of men, Henry concludes; but if God be our friend he will not fail us in the time of need. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job has now been abandoned to the very centre of his life, and that a man so emptied of every human love is being driven, by the exhaustion of all lesser refuges, toward the one Friend who does not turn away.
20:
Turning from the ruin of his friendships to the ruin of his frame, Job says, my bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. The reformed John Gill reads the first clause of a body wasted to nothing: as his bones used to be covered and clothed with flesh, now the flesh is consumed away with disease and grief, so that the bones stick to the skin and are seen through it — Job reduced to a mere skeleton, skin and bone, by the force of his bodily disorder and the anguish of his mind together.

The famous second clause, escaped with the skin of my teeth, the witnesses handle as a proverb of the narrowest deliverance. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes it so: Job's flesh is entirely wasted, nothing but skin and bone left, and if he still lives at all it is a wonder — he has had as narrow an escape from death as the thickness of the enamel on the teeth, within a hair's breadth of destruction. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that the words have passed into a proverb for a very narrow escape, though he confesses the phrase is far from clear in its context; some, he notes, explain it that Job escaped only with the skin of his teeth because the teeth alone have no skin, and others because his teeth themselves had fallen out — a meaning to be got only by inference from this one place. Keil and Delitzsch group the verse with the entreaty that follows, hearing Job's natural strength grow feebler and his voice weaker as the description of his suffering sinks toward the piteous appeal about to be made.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the wasted body as the last of the comforts stripped from Job. When those about him slighted him, had he been in health and at ease he might yet have enjoyed himself; but he could take as little pleasure in himself as others took in him, for his bone cleaved now to his skin as formerly it clove to his flesh, and he was a perfect skeleton, nothing but skin and bones. See, Henry says, what little reason we have to indulge the body, which, after all our care, may be thus consumed by the diseases it carries in its own seeds. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, forsaken by every friend, is now failing in his own flesh as well, so wasted that his survival is itself a marvel — and it is out of just this extremity, a man barely clinging to a ruined body, that the great confession of an incorruptible hope is about to rise.
21:
Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me — and the witnesses hear the doubled cry as the most melting note Job has yet struck. The reformed John Gill reads the repetition as the very pulse of his distress: the phrase is doubled to mark the vehemence of his affliction, the ardency of his soul, the anguish of his spirit, and his earnest longing to be pitied; and in it, Gill thinks, Job not only begs compassion of his friends but gently reproves their want of it, for his case called for pity, not for calumny and censure. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says the same of the iteration — it strongly indicates the depth of his distress, and that his spirit was worn down by the length and severity of his suffering.

The grammatical-historical witnesses feel the change of tone. Keil and Delitzsch note that Job here takes up a strain not heard before: his strength grows more and more feeble, his voice weaker and weaker, and a feeling of sadness now stamps the address to the friends with a tone of importunate entreaty meant, if possible, to reach their heart — for they are indeed his friends, as the emphatic O ye my friends insists even while it pleads. Charles Ellicott marks it as an exceeding great and bitter cry, of a piece with the appeal at ch. 16:20.

The ground of the plea, all the witnesses agree, is in the last clause: for the hand of God hath touched me. John Wesley reads it of the inward wound — Job's spirit is touched with a sense of God's wrath, a calamity of all others the most grievous. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes it the heart of the appeal and begs it in language, he says, enough to break a heart of stone: have pity upon me, O ye my friends; if you will do nothing else for me, be sorry for me, and show some concern; for the hand of God hath touched me. His case was sad indeed, Henry says, for he had fallen into the hands of the living God, his spirit touched with the sense of his wrath; and it becomes friends to pity one another in trouble, and not to shut up the bowels of compassion. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, having exhausted every argument, falls back on the simplest and most human of pleas — not vindicate me but pity me — and grounds even that on the awful fact that it is God's own hand which has laid him so low.
22:
The plea for pity turns to a reproach when the friends will give none: why do ye persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh? The reformed John Gill fastens on the strange phrase as God. God, being sovereign, may pursue and hunt a man with one affliction after another and is accountable to none; but men are not therefore warranted to do the like, nor is all that God does a precedent for us — we are to be merciful as he is merciful, not to afflict his people because he does. God had persecuted Job, hunting him as a fierce lion hunts its prey; that was no reason his friends should join the chase.

The wesleyan-arminian voices read the two clauses as body and soul. Adam Clarke: are not the afflictions God sends enough? do ye not see I have as much as I can bear? — and then, will ye persecute my soul while God is persecuting my body? is it not enough that my body is destroyed, but you must labour to torment my mind? John Wesley reads as God of the friends' presumption to a divine knowledge and authority — as if they had God's own power to search his heart and know his hypocrisy, and God's sovereign right to do with him what they pleased; and not satisfied with my flesh he takes of beasts of prey that are not content to devour the flesh but must break the very bones. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply refers the language back to Job's earlier cry of being torn as by an enemy at ch. 16:9.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, stand at this verse on the threshold of the great confession, and here begin to lay out how they will construe it. Reading upon the dust at v.25 as they do, they hold that this speech does not express a hope of bodily recovery at all; and they render the coming lines starkly — that after his skin is thus torn to pieces, and without his flesh, Job shall behold God, whom he shall behold for his good while his very reins languish within him. It is a reading, set down thus early, that will divide the witnesses sharply when the confession itself is reached. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the reproach at hand: why do you persecute me as God? his rebukes are surely enough for one man to bear; you need not add your wormwood and gall to the cup of affliction he puts into my hand. God, Henry says, may do what he pleases with Job and give account of none of his matters, but the friends must give account of theirs; we are to aim to be like the most holy and most merciful, not like the most high and most mighty. The witnesses do not divide over the plea; they agree that Job asks his friends only to leave the persecuting to God, and to spare the wounded flesh God has already wasted.
23:
Between his complaint and his confession Job pauses to wish his words made permanent: oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! The reformed John Gill is careful which words Job means — not the transactions of his life, nor merely the defences already made, but the words he is about to deliver, his confession of a living Redeemer, of the resurrection, and of a future state; these he wishes written, that they might remain as a standing testimony of his faith, for what is written abides when what is only spoken is soon forgotten. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes the occasion to correct the translation: the verb rendered printed should be described or traced out, for printing was unknown for nearly two thousand years after Job; what Job names are the writing-modes of his own day — the book of papyrus or linen, the letters cut with an iron stile on plates of lead, the words engraved on rock — and Clarke marshals Pliny and Pausanias to show that men wrote first on palm-leaves and then on bark, lead, and stone.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that these three verses are manifestly more emphatic than any Job has yet spoken, and finds no reason why it should not be especially these very words he longs above all others to have recorded; the now, he suggests, means here, and points to the confession at hand. John Wesley notes the quiet providence in the wish, that what Job desired God granted: his words are written in God's book, so that wherever that book is read this glorious confession is declared for a memorial of him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lingers here longest, for in all the conferences he finds no lines more weighty. Here is much both of Christ and of heaven; he that said such things declared plainly that he sought the better country, that is, the heavenly, as the patriarchs did (Heb. 11:14). Job was now accused, and this was his appeal; now afflicted, and this his cordial. Henry reckons him just now under an extraordinary impulse of the blessed Spirit, raised above himself and given light and utterance to his own surprise; and he observes that after this we do not find Job's discourses so passionate and despairing as before — this hope quieted his spirit and stilled the storm, and having here cast anchor within the veil his mind was kept steady from that time forward. So Job breaks off his complaint abruptly, Henry says, to triumph in his comfort, not for his own satisfaction only but for the edification of others, wishing it recorded plainly and printed, put into a book, or engraven with an iron pen in the rock, for a perpetual memorial to the generations to come. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the solemn preface marks the summit of the book — a man who has lost everything staking all on words he would have outlast the very rock.
24:
The wish for permanence rises to its height: that they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever. The reformed John Gill weighs how the instruments go together. Not that both iron and lead were pens, for the marks of a leaden pencil are neither durable nor fit for a rock; rather the words might be written with an iron stile upon a sheet of lead — for the ancients, as Pliny relates, made books and engrossed public records on sheets of lead for their permanence — or else the letters might be cut into stone and the incisions filled up with molten lead poured in, as Jarchi suggested, to make them stand out plain and lasting. Gill recalls Pliny's mention of stone pillars in Arabia inscribed with unknown characters, the very kind of enduring monument Job seems to covet.

The wesleyan-arminian voices settle the same question of method. Adam Clarke reports the common supposition that the iron pen is the chisel by which the letters were deeply cut, and the lead melted into the cavities to preserve the engraving distinct; but he judges it more natural to take Job as simply naming the several kinds of writing used in his time, and rests the point on his quotations from Pliny and Pausanias. John Wesley states it plainly: anciently they used to grave the letters in a stone with an iron tool, and then to fill up the cuts with lead, that the words might be more plainly seen.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance, and the very concreteness of their debate serves the verse's feeling. Job is not asking for ink on a page that fire or time might waste, but for the most nearly imperishable record his age could imagine — iron biting into rock, the furrows sealed with lead, the inscription set up for ever. It is the language of a man who knows his body is wasting to dust and his memory threatened, as Bildad had threatened, with extinction, and who therefore reaches past his own frailty for something that will outlast him and speak when he is gone. And what he would so engrave is not his sufferings or his self-defence but the three great sentences that follow; the witnesses read this verse as the deep breath before them, Job piling permanence on permanence — book, lead, rock, and for ever — so that the confession of his Redeemer might stand as a witness to every generation that should come after. The care he spends on the monument measures the worth he sets on the words about to be cut into it.
25:
For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth — the mountain-peak of the book, and the place where the witnesses divide most sharply, over the very identity of the Redeemer. The reformed John Gill argues the word down to one meaning. The goel is the next of kin, to whom by the law of Lev. 25:25 belonged the right of redeeming a mortgaged estate; but Job cannot mean any mere man that should rise up to vindicate him, for such a one could not be said to live and to stand at the latter day upon the earth; nor God the Father, to whom the name Redeemer is scarcely given and who never stood on earth; but the Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it the same way and richly: there is a Redeemer provided for fallen man, and Jesus Christ is that Redeemer; our heavenly inheritance was mortgaged by sin, and Christ, our near kinsman, is the one able to redeem it. He is a living Redeemer, almighty and eternal; and Job, having lost wealth and friends, was not cut off from his interest in him — still he is my Redeemer.

The wesleyan-arminian voices join this confession. John Wesley presses that the goel most fitly agrees to Christ, our nearest kinsman, who took our nature, redeemed the lost inheritance by his own blood, avenged our death upon the devil, and preserves our name for ever; and he marks that after these words Job's impatient and despairing passages cease, as though the hope had breathed new life into him. Adam Clarke, having weighed at length whether the passage speaks of a future resurrection and redemption by Christ or only of Job's restoration to health and prosperity in this life, comes down firmly for the former: Job spoke under the special inspiration of the Spirit, and a revelation by which the whole human race might be benefited is worthier of such a moment than one touching Job's private welfare; my Redeemer, goali, is his Kinsman who has the right of redemption, and liveth, chai, is the living One who holds the keys of death.

The grammatical-historical witnesses hold back from naming Christ so directly, and read the Redeemer as God himself. Charles Ellicott traces the ascent of Job's longing — for a daysman at ch. 9:33, a witness in heaven at ch. 16:19, a surety at ch. 17:3 — and says that here Job goes a step further and knows he has a goel, whose various functions God will take upon himself: God will avenge his quarrel, be surety for him, and vindicate him before men and before God. This alone, Ellicott says, is a marvellous confession, for it states the reality and eternity of God and is faith in the I am; his Vindicator liveth, exists now, and shall stand last upon earth after all others have passed away (Isa. 40:8). And upon the earth is literally upon dust, the word used again at ch. 41:33 — a usage, he insists, that tells strongly against the rendering over my dust. Keil and Delitzsch render the line as the last One will He arise from the dust, and warn that, so construed, the verse holds out no hope of bodily recovery. So the debate stands unresolved: is the living Redeemer the incarnate Christ who shall stand at the last day, as the reformed, puritan, and wesleyan voices confess, or God himself the eternal Vindicator, as the grammatical-historical voices more guardedly read? The witnesses divide, yet all confess a Redeemer who liveth, and Job's own emphatic I know rings over the whole dispute.
26:
The confession presses through the grave itself: and though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God. Here the sharpest grammatical division of the chapter opens, over the little Hebrew min-basari — from or out of my flesh. The reformed John Gill takes it of bodily resurrection: when Job is wholly stripped of his skin in the grave, and rottenness and worms have consumed the rest of his flesh and bones, so that his body is utterly destroyed, yet even so he is assured he shall rise. The wesleyan-arminian voices read it the same way and press the point home. Adam Clarke paraphrases, I shall arise from the dead, have a renewed body, and see him with eyes of flesh and blood, though what I have now shall shortly moulder into dust; and he notes the precise words, that they — diseases and afflictions — destroy this, the word body being supplied. John Wesley is fullest: though his skin is in great measure consumed, and the rest of it with this body shall be devoured by worms, yet with bodily eyes, his flesh raised from the grave and reunited to his soul, he shall see God — and not by a bare seeing, but in that glorious and beatifying vision promised to all God's people.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry stands with them and draws it out. Job counts upon the corrupting of his body in the grave with a holy carelessness; yet in my flesh shall I see God — soul and body shall come together again, the same body that died raised a glorious and spiritual body (1 Cor. 15:44), and Job and God shall come together too, Job seeing the glorified Redeemer who is God. This, Henry insists, must be understood of the redemption of Job's soul from the power of the grave and his reception to glory (Ps. 49:15), not of any temporal deliverance, for Job had just said his way was fenced up and his hope removed like a tree, and elsewhere despaired of all comfort in this life; the forced strain of the words if read of a temporal rescue confirms that he speaks of the resurrection.

Against this stands the grammatical-historical reading. Keil and Delitzsch construe min as privative — and without my flesh shall I behold Eloah — so that Job looks to see God not clothed in a risen body but stripped of the flesh altogether, his spirit beholding God after the body has been torn to pieces; on their view no hope of bodily recovery, and perhaps none of bodily resurrection, is expressed in the line. Charles Ellicott holds the phrase in a careful balance: after my skin hath been destroyed, even from my flesh I shall see God may refer first to Job's present faith — that notwithstanding the corruption of his disease he can and does still see God, whom he knows as his Redeemer — or it may point to something yet to come, when the Redeemer stands at the last upon the earth. The witnesses do not resolve it: in the flesh, a body raised and glorified, or without the flesh, a spirit beholding God, or a present sight of God kept even amid decay. Yet through every rendering the same certainty holds — that the destruction of his flesh, so far from ending Job's vision of God, is the very threshold of it.
27:
Job dwells on the sight with a lover's repetition: whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another. The reformed John Gill reads it of a seeing that is all Job's own — for his own pleasure and profit, to his great advantage and inexpressible joy. The wesleyan-arminian voices press the personal note. Adam Clarke fixes on not another, the Hebrew zar, not a stranger — not one who has no relation to human nature, but his redeeming Kinsman; Job shall have a personal interest in the resurrection as he has in the Redeemer, and his own eyes shall behold that very One who is both the resurrection and the life. John Wesley hears why Job repeats himself: no wonder he says it again, the meditation being most sweet to him; for myself, for my own benefit and comfort, and not another for me — I shall not see God by another's eyes but by my own, by these self-same eyes, in this same body which now I have.

The last clause, though my reins be consumed within me, the witnesses take of Job's longing and his frailty at once. Keil and Delitzsch render it my veins languish in my bosom, hearing the confession sink again toward the weakness of the wasted man even as it soars; Clarke reads it that Job is now apparently on the brink of death, the thread of life spun out to extreme tenuity; and Matthew Henry, the puritan-evangelical voice, hears in it Job's whole desire summed up and concluded — all my longings are gathered into this, that I shall see him; let me have this, and I have nothing more to desire.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the honest question the verses raise: do Job's words then teach the resurrection? Possibly not directly, he answers, but they express the firm conviction of that faith of which the resurrection is the only natural justification — a living trust in a living personal God who, coming into contact with man, cannot suffer his Holy One to see corruption. How far Job believed in a resurrection of the flesh hereafter Ellicott will not say; but he certainly believed in life out of death and through death here, and no man can believe in a living God and not believe that God must triumph over death. It is possible, Ellicott adds, to hold some dogma about the resurrection and yet not believe in God; in this Job was unlike us, and for this reason his confession rightly stands at the head of the Christian burial office, which looks forward to the resurrection and lays fast hold on it. The witnesses do not finally divide over the sweetness of the hope, only over its reach: whether Job here sees, with the reformed and wesleyan voices, his own risen eyes beholding God, or, with Ellicott, holds the faith of which such a resurrection is the sure and only fitting fruit. Either way, the man dying in his flesh has fixed his gaze on a God he means to see and keep in sight for ever.
28:
The confession made, Job turns its edge back upon his accusers, telling them what they ought to say: but ye should say, why persecute we him, seeing the root of the matter is found in me? The reformed John Gill reads it as Job directing his friends to the use they should now make of his creed — to say within themselves and to one another that they had done wrong to hound a man in whom the root of true religion was plainly found. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears in it a coming repentance: then ye shall say, how did we persecute him! we are now convinced that we did wrong, since the root of the matter — a pure practice and a sound hope resting on sound faith received from God — is found in him. Clarke notes too a textual point, that more than a hundred manuscripts and several versions read in him rather than in me, so that the friends confess the root of the matter to be found in Job.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets out the verse's real difficulty, which turns on what the root of the matter means — the cause of Job's suffering, or the essence of piety. He judges it preferable to render, for ye say, what is a persecuted man to God? why should he persecute any man without cause? and therefore the root of the matter — that is, the cause of the afflictions — must be found in me; on this reading the clause states the friends' cruel logic rather than their coming repentance. John Wesley keeps to the other sense: the root denotes a root of true religion, and the root of all true religion is a living faith, which the friends should own to be in Job because his faith and hope are in God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into counsel for both parties. It is a word of caution to the friends not to persist in their unkind usage — why persecute we him, seeing the root of the matter is found in him? — and Henry turns it inward: we are all concerned to see that the root of the matter be in us, a living, quickening, commanding principle of grace in the heart, as necessary to our religion as the root to the tree; love to God and our brethren, faith in Christ, hatred of sin — these are the root of the matter, and other things but leaves in comparison. And it directs our conduct toward others, that many have the root of the matter in them who are not in everything of our mind, and it is at our peril if we persecute such. Job and his friends differed about the methods of Providence, Henry notes, but agreed in the root of the matter, the belief of another world, and therefore should not have persecuted one another for their differences. The witnesses divide over the grammar of the clause but not over its drift; they agree that Job bids his friends read his confession as proof that the essential thing was in him all along, and let their persecuting cease.
29:
The chapter closes not in complaint but in solemn warning: be ye afraid of the sword: for wrath bringeth the punishments of the sword, that ye may know there is a judgment. The reformed John Gill reads the sword not of the civil magistrate nor of a foreign foe but of avenging divine justice, lest God should whet the glittering sword of his justice and take hold on judgment to avenge the wrongs of the innocent — unless the other swords too be reckoned his instruments. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke warns the friends that such anger as they have shown against Job, God will certainly resent and punish; and by that ye may know there is a judgment Job would have them learn that God will judge the world, and that the unequal distribution of good and ill in this present life is itself a proof that a future judgment must come, where evil shall be punished and virtue rewarded.

Clarke also reports, in fairness, a third reading of the whole confession, proposed by Kennicott, which neither of the two great opinions had allowed. Kennicott held that Job here expresses neither a firm belief in a resurrection to happiness after death, nor a hope of restoration to prosperity in this life — since Job elsewhere insists his death is near — but a divine conviction, just then revealed to him, that out of his wasted body, in his flesh thus stripped of skin and near the grave, he should see God appear to vindicate the integrity of his character before his friends and the world; a vindication which the close of the book, where God calls Job his servant and rebukes the three, is thought to confirm. Clarke sets down Kennicott's new version, with its my Vindicator liveth and its he shall arise over this dust, but candidly judges the theory better than the arguments that support it, and the version itself more than the Hebrew text will bear; he holds still to the reading of a future resurrection and redemption by Christ.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the verse a word of terror to men found smiting their fellow-servant, as Christ warned in Matt. 24:49. Good men, he says, need sometimes to be frightened from sin by the terrors of the Almighty, and particularly from the sin of rashly judging their brethren (Matt. 7:1; Jam. 3:1); those who are peevish and censorious toward their brethren should know that their wrath works not the righteousness of God, and may bring on them the very sword they threatened, and worse behind it if they repent not. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the sword of some considerable judgment to be inflicted on them, and the whole as an admonition given in time that they might prevent it, for God observes and will judge all their words and actions. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, having anchored his own soul in a living Redeemer and a coming judgment, turns to his accusers with the same judgment as a warning — that the God who will vindicate the innocent will also reckon with those who persecuted him, and that the certainty of a judgment to come is at once his comfort and their peril.
